abstracts.abstract: This paper establishes a unified information-theoretic framework for non-stationary and non-ergodic sources, addressing a fundamental limitation in classical Shannon theory. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on stationarity assumptions, we introduce a novel entropy measure termed ``variational information rate'' that captures the time-varying statistical structure of general sources. The central contribution lies in establishing a general source coding theorem that characterizes the fundamental limits of compression for these sources, revealing that the minimal achievable rate equals the supremum of the variational information rate over all time-averaging windows. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed framework naturally subsumes existing theories for i.i.d., Markov, and stationary sources as special cases, thereby providing a unifying perspective that bridges previously disparate research directions. Our analysis reveals unexpected connections between source coding and hypothesis testing in non-stationary regimes. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world non-stationary data sources confirm that the theoretical bounds are tight and that conventional stationary-based coding schemes suffer significant performance degradation. This work opens new avenues for information theory in modern applications involving time-varying data streams, such as IoT sensor networks and adaptive multimedia compression.

This paper derives significantly tighter inner and outer bounds on the capacity region of the K-user Gaussian multiple access channel (GMAC), advancing the state-of-the-art understanding of multi-user information theory. While existing bounds capture the general structure of the capacity region, they exhibit substantial gaps, particularly in the high SNR regime and for asymmetric user configurations. Our approach introduces novel auxiliary random variables and a refined analysis of the relationship between superposition coding and rate splitting. For the outer bound, we establish a new inequality relating the mutual information terms that provides a tighter characterization of the capacity constraints. For the inner bound, we prove that a modified superposition coding scheme with carefully optimized power allocations achieves rates strictly exceeding those of prior constructions. In the symmetric case, our bounds coincide, thereby establishing the exact capacity region. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that the improvement over existing bounds is substantial: for a two-user GMAC with unequal channel gains, the capacity sum-rate gap is reduced from O(1/log SNR) to O(1/(log SNR)^2). These results have direct implications for the design of practical multi-user communication systems and provide sharper guidelines for resource allocation in cellular networks.

This paper proposes a fundamentally new approach to joint source-channel coding for visual communications, departing from the traditional separate source and channel coding paradigm that has dominated since Shannon's separation principle. The proposed system, termed ``semantic-aware unequal error protection coding,'' jointly optimizes source representation and channel coding by exploiting semantic information at multiple abstraction levels of image data. The key innovation lies in a novel rate-adaptive semantic encoder that identifies and prioritizes perceptually critical image structures, combined with a flexible channel code that provides unequal protection levels matched to the semantic importance of different code segments. Unlike conventional systems that treat all bits equally, our design introduces a three-tier protection scheme where critical semantic features receive maximum redundancy while redundant texture information is transmitted with minimal overhead. We implement the system using deep neural network-based semantic extraction and polar codes for channel coding. Extensive experiments over wireless channels with varying SNR and fading conditions demonstrate that the proposed system achieves 3-5 dB PSNR improvement over state-of-the-art JPEG2000 and HEVC-based transmission schemes at the same bandwidth, with particularly pronounced gains for high-motion video content. The architecture enables graceful degradation under adverse channel conditions while fully exploiting favorable conditions.

This paper presents an optimized polar coding scheme specifically designed for the control channel in massive machine-type communications (mMTC), addressing critical challenges in next-generation IoT deployment scenarios. Existing polar code constructions for control channels assume homogeneous channel conditions, which fail to capture the heterogeneous interference patterns inherent in dense mMTC environments with sporadic traffic. Our proposed scheme introduces a novel ``dynamic frozen set adaptation'' mechanism that adjusts the frozen bit pattern based on real-time collision and interference estimation, enabling robust communication under highly variable channel conditions. The key technical contributions include: (1) a low-complexity algorithm for dynamic frozen set computation that maintains O(N log N) decoding complexity, (2) an adaptive encoding strategy that exploits partial channel state information available at the transmitter, and (3) a distributed contention resolution protocol integrated with polar coding that substantially reduces collision probability. Implementation results on a software-defined radio platform demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a 40% reduction in control channel decoding latency compared to standardized 5G polar codes while maintaining comparable block error rate performance. In simulated mMTC scenarios with 1000 devices per cell, the system achieves a 25% improvement in access success rate under heavy load conditions, validating the practical viability for massive IoT deployments.
